units.canonical_text: See how private IPv4 egress depends on a NAT host. With no public IP, the workload uses its default route to the NAT instance in a public subnet. That subnet routes to the internet gateway; replies return through the NAT host.

units.canonical_text: The NAT instance needs a public address, shown here as an Elastic IP, and must be configured to forward packets and do source NAT. Its source and destination check is disabled because it handles packets addressed to other hosts.
units.speech_text: The nat instance needs a public address, shown here as an Elastic I P, and must be configured to forward packets and do source nat. Its source and destination check is disabled because it handles packets addressed to other hosts.

units.canonical_text: If this host stops, private IPv4 egress fails in this design. There is no automatic failover here. With an instance, you own patching, sizing, security and recovery. A managed NAT gateway shifts service operations to AWS, but you still design for resilience.

units.canonical_text: Choose link aggregation to add capacity and link redundancy, not endpoint diversity. A link aggregation group bundles dedicated connections at the same Direct Connect endpoint into one logical interface. Link Aggregation Control Protocol manages the member links.
units.speech_text: A link aggregation group bundles dedicated connections at the same Direct Connect endpoint into one logical interface. Link Aggregation Control Protocol manages member links. This improves total capacity and link redundancy, but the members still share endpoint failure exposure.

units.canonical_text: Direct Connect is primary; a separate internet IPsec VPN is the recovery path. Do not assume the backup has the same capacity or that the two paths share the same failure boundary.

units.canonical_text: Site-to-Site IPsec protects packets between the VPN gateways. Its protection ends at those gateways. It doesn't, by itself, protect every application hop outside that tunnel.
